title: Getting Started with React Hooks
excerpt: A beginner-friendly walkthrough of useState and useEffect, and why hooks changed the way we write React components.
content:
Hooks let you use state and other React features without writing a class. The two most common hooks are useState and useEffect.

useState gives a component local state, while useEffect lets you run side effects such as fetching data or subscribing to events after render.

Start small: convert one class component at a time, and keep your effects focused on a single concern.

title: JavaScript Array Methods You Should Know
excerpt: map, filter, reduce, and a few lesser-known array methods that make everyday JavaScript cleaner.
content:
map, filter, and reduce cover most day-to-day transformations, but methods like find, some, and flatMap are worth knowing too.

Prefer these over manual for loops when you're transforming or querying a list — they read closer to the intent of the code.

title: Mastering CSS Grid Layout
excerpt: How to think in rows and columns with CSS Grid, and when to reach for Grid instead of Flexbox.
content:
CSS Grid excels at two-dimensional layouts — rows and columns at the same time — while Flexbox is better suited to one-dimensional layouts.

Define a grid-template-columns and grid-template-areas to lay out a page skeleton in just a few lines of CSS.

title: WordPress Theme Development Basics
excerpt: An introduction to template hierarchy, functions.php, and building your first custom WordPress theme.
content:
Every WordPress theme starts with style.css and index.php. From there, the template hierarchy decides which file renders a given page.

Use functions.php to register menus, widget areas, and theme support features like custom logos and post thumbnails.

title: Building REST APIs with Node.js
excerpt: A practical guide to structuring routes, controllers, and middleware for a clean Express API.
content:
A well-structured Express API separates routes, controllers, and middleware so each file has one job.

Add centralized error handling early — it keeps your controllers small and your error responses consistent.

title: Why Clean Code Matters
excerpt: Clean code isn't about perfection - it's about making the next change easier for whoever touches the code next.
content:
Clean code favors clarity over cleverness. Descriptive names, small functions, and consistent formatting all pay off the moment someone else (including future you) needs to change the code.

Treat readability as a feature, not an afterthought.

title: React Performance Optimization Tips
excerpt: Practical techniques - memoization, code splitting, and virtualization - for keeping React apps fast.
content:
Reach for React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback only when profiling shows a real re-render problem — premature memoization adds complexity without benefit.

For large lists, list virtualization and route-based code splitting usually give a bigger win than micro-optimizations.

title: Understanding Async/Await in JavaScript
excerpt: How async/await builds on Promises to make asynchronous code read like synchronous code.
content:
async/await is syntax sugar over Promises — an async function always returns a Promise, and await pauses execution until that Promise settles.

Wrap awaited calls in try/catch to handle rejections the same way you'd handle a thrown error.

title: React Server Components in Plain English
excerpt: What Server Components actually are, how they differ from SSR, and when they're worth reaching for.
content:
A Server Component renders entirely on the server and ships zero JavaScript to the browser for that piece of the tree — it's not the same thing as server-side rendering, which still hydrates on the client.

Reach for Server Components for data-heavy, mostly-static pieces of a page, and keep 'use client' components for anything that needs state, effects, or event handlers.

title: A Practical Guide to CSS Custom Properties
excerpt: Using CSS variables for theming, spacing scales, and component state instead of hardcoded values.
content:
CSS custom properties (--like-this) aren't just for colors — they're great for spacing scales, breakpoints, and even passing values from JavaScript into CSS via element.style.setProperty().

Scope a variable to a component root instead of :root when it only needs to vary locally, and it becomes a lightweight way to theme one part of a page without extra classes.

title: Designing Idempotent APIs
excerpt: Why idempotency matters for retries and flaky networks, and how to add idempotency keys to your endpoints.
content:
An idempotent endpoint returns the same result no matter how many times a client retries the same request — essential once you're dealing with real networks that drop responses, not just requests.

For POST endpoints that create resources, accept a client-generated Idempotency-Key header and store the result keyed on it so a retried request returns the original response instead of creating a duplicate.

title: Debugging Memory Leaks in JavaScript Apps
excerpt: How to use the Chrome DevTools heap snapshot to find detached DOM nodes and forgotten event listeners.
content:
Most front-end memory leaks come down to a handful of causes: event listeners that are never removed, timers that outlive the component that created them, and closures holding a reference to DOM nodes that were already removed.

Take two heap snapshots in DevTools — before and after the suspected leaky action — and compare them; a growing count of Detached HTMLDivElement nodes is a strong signal something isn't cleaning up after itself.

title: Securing a WordPress Site: The Essentials
excerpt: The handful of changes that stop most automated WordPress attacks before they start.
content:
Keep WordPress core, themes, and plugins updated, remove any plugin you're not actively using, and disable file editing from the admin dashboard with define('DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true); in wp-config.php.

Beyond that, a unique database prefix, strong admin passwords with two-factor auth, and regular offsite backups cover the vast majority of real-world attacks.

title: How We Review Pull Requests
excerpt: A short, practical checklist for giving useful code review feedback without slowing the team down.
content:
A good review comments on the behavior and risk of a change before it comments on style — naming and formatting nits are worth raising, but they shouldn't block a merge on their own.

Keep pull requests small enough to review in one sitting; a 40-line diff gets a careful review, a 1,200-line diff gets a rubber stamp.

title: State Management Without Redux
excerpt: When useState, useReducer, and Context are genuinely enough, and how to tell you've outgrown them.
content:
Most apps don't need a global state library — useState and useReducer handle local state, and Context handles the occasional value that needs to skip a few levels, like the current theme or logged-in user.

Reach for a dedicated state library once you have state that many unrelated components read and write at high frequency, and prop drilling or re-render cost actually becomes a measured problem.

title: Container Queries Are Finally Usable
excerpt: Styling a component based on its container's size instead of the viewport, with broad browser support.
content:
Container queries let a component adapt to the space it's actually given, not the size of the browser window — wrap it in a container with container-type: inline-size, then style with @container.

This finally makes truly reusable components possible: the same card can lay out differently in a narrow sidebar and a wide main column without any JavaScript.
